analysis.one_liner: Requires states to draw congressional maps using nonpartisan independent commissions instead of politicians.
analysis.headline: One Republican and five House Democrats backed the bill; it was sent to the Judiciary Committee, which has taken no action on it since January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would take the drawing of congressional district lines away from state politicians and give it to independent commissions with an even partisan balance and no elected officials on them. States that refuse to make the same change for their own legislative districts would lose federal election-administration money. Fairer maps make it harder for the party in power to draw itself safe seats, which supporters say makes representatives answer to voters instead of party leaders.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters, especially in states where one party currently draws its own district lines. Independent commissions tend to produce maps that are less skewed toward whichever party holds power at map-drawing time, more competitive districts, and representatives who have to appeal to a broader range of voters to keep their seats.

how_it_helps.text: Requires every state to conduct congressional redistricting through a nonpartisan independent commission, beginning with the redistricting done after the 2020 census [S3].
A commission counts as nonpartisan and independent only if members are split evenly between the state's two largest parties and no member is an elected public official [S3].

A state cannot use federal funds provided for election administration unless it certifies to the Election Assistance Commission that it also uses an independent commission for its state legislative districts [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Incumbent members of Congress and state legislators, and the party organizations that currently control redistricting, would give up their power to draw their own district lines and would face a real risk of losing safe seats. States that keep politician-drawn maps would forgo federal election-administration funding.

drawbacks.text: The requirement applies 'beginning with the redistricting carried out pursuant to the 2020 census,' which is already past; Congress cannot retroactively redo maps drawn years earlier, so the provision as written is legally questionable and the next real test would be the 2030 census [S3].

Conditioning federal election-administration money on adopting a state-level commission effectively pressures states into a one-size-fits-all process, an approach critics say intrudes on state authority over their own legislatures [S3].

A commission defined only by even partisan balance and the exclusion of elected officials can still be gamed through member selection, and states with true tripartisan or nonpartisan voter rolls may not fit the two-party formula [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — no politician draws the district they run in — has broad public support and directly targets the self-interest of the people who would have to vote for it. The bill's main weakness is drafting, not concept: it applies to a redistricting cycle that has already happened, and its funding penalty for states is blunt. A well-built version would set the standard for the 2030 census; this version reads more as a statement of principle than a workable law.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee in January 2025, and the committee has not scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it since.

narrative.text: Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, a Pennsylvania Republican, introduced the bill on January 3, 2025, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S1].
Five House Democrats signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill backing from both parties [S4].
The bill's only recorded actions are its introduction and referral; no hearing, markup, or floor vote appears in the action history [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent officeholders and party organizations keep the power to draw their own congressional district lines, which is exactly what the bill would have taken from them. The public gets no change in how maps are drawn.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Incumbents who draw their own districts

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only backers on record are one Republican sponsor and five Democratic cosponsors, so it has support from both parties but very little of it; no one is on record opposing it because the committee has simply not acted.

industries.note: Redistricting power currently sits with the politicians who then run in the districts they drew. The bill would move map-drawing to balanced independent commissions with no elected officials on them, removing a major built-in advantage for incumbents and the party in power.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has sat in committee without action for roughly a year and has only six total supporters in the House. With both parties currently engaged in aggressive map-drawing battles to their own benefit, the near-certain path is that the bill dies in committee at the end of this Congress unless it is reintroduced in the next one.
